transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alexei (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Maya (VectorHealth Head of Security), Devon (Platform Eng), Priya (Compliance)

Summary:
High-level deep dive on private deployment architecture: control-plane placement, network isolation patterns, ingress/egress controls, key management integration, audit log flows and compliance evidence. Customer emphasized strict data residency and need for isolated control plane or air-gapped control signals.

Topics: control plane (managed vs customer-hosted), VPC peering vs Transit Gateway, egress proxy placement, KMS/HSM integration and key rotation, SIEM/log-forwarding, RBAC & SSO mapping, SOC2 evidence export.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alexei: Hey everyone, thanks for joining—uh sorry for the slight delay. This is Alexei from Redwood, AE on the account. Today Samira and I will run through network and control plane options for a private deployment.
[00:18] Maya: Thanks Alexei. We re— we have a couple of constraints: data must remain in our EU region, control signals should not traverse public internet, and audit logs need to land in our SIEM with seven year retention, ideally immutable.
[00:36] Samira: Great, noted. We'll cover patterns that avoid public egress for model payloads and options for a customer-hosted control plane. Quick question — do you currently have a Transit Gateway setup across all accounts?
[00:52] Devon: We do, yes. TGW connects our prod and restricted accounts, but anything flagged as PII must live in a restricted VPC with no peering to sandbox.
[01:08] Alexei: Perfect. For private we typically recommend two patterns—either Redwood control plane in customer's VPC (private control plane) or a customer-hosted control plane. Both can be configured so model runtime is entirely in your restricted VPC.
[01:26] Maya: When you say "private control plane in our VPC" — where do keys live? We need hardware-backed keys, FIPS 140-2 / HSM.
[01:40] Samira: Great question. For that pattern Redwood integrates with your KMS; we can support cloud KMS providers (Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS) and bring-your-own-HSM via PKCS#11 or Cloud HSM integrations. The customer-managed keys can remain in your tenant—Redwood never persists plaintext keys.
[01:58] Priya: Do you support key rotation policies and key usage auditing so auditors can confirm rotation cadence?
[02:08] Samira: Yes. We log all KMS operations to the audit stream — encrypt/decrypt requests, key rotations, IAM actions. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via our log-connector or pushed to an S3/GCS bucket with an object-lock retention policy.
[02:24] Maya: There was another architecture we considered — isolated runtime with a minimal outbound egress channel only to a firm egress proxy. Does Redwood need DNS resolution externally?
[02:36] Alexei: The runtime itself needs to reach the control plane for configuration and model discovery. If you choose customer-hosted control plane within the same VPC, that channel can be entirely internal and mTLS protected. For hosted control plane options we support private link-like constructs and egress proxies to avoid public internet.
[02:56] Devon: Ok, so if we could host the control plane internal, then traffic stays within TGW and doesn't hit public internet. How do you recommend NAT vs egress-proxy?
[03:12] Samira: NAT is simpler but it leaves you with broader egress surface; an egress-proxy (squid/varnish or our managed egress appliance) gives you strict allowlisting for minimal domains, TLS interception if you permit, and better auditing. We usually recommend an egress-proxy for high-security customers.
[03:30] Maya: We also have to show auditors RBAC mapping from our IdP to Redwood roles. How does SSO work with private?
[03:40] Alexei: SSO is SAML/OpenID Connect. We can federate with Okta/Azure AD. For private control plane deployments we run the control-plane auth tier in your network, and you configure the IdP trust to that endpoint. Role mapping is via SAML attributes; we provide a mapping table that maps VectorHealth groups to Redwood roles.
[03:58] Priya: Is there an API-level service account pattern for automation, and can those be rotated automatically?
[04:08] Samira: Yes, service accounts are supported; tokens can be short-lived and rotated via your existing secrets manager. We support automatic token refresh and integration with Vault for dynamic credentials.
[04:20] [00:04:20] Speaker 1: (inaudible) question about logging format — do you support common schema?
[04:28] Samira: We emit structured JSON logs with fields for requestID, userID, modelID, tokens_in/tokens_out, KMS-correlation id, and a sha-like request fingerprint. That maps cleanly into Splunk/ELK/Datadog.
[04:44] Devon: For audit retention, object lock is fine for raw request logs, but we have to scrubbing PII in some cases. How do you handle redaction?
[04:56] Samira: We can scrub prompt text at the ingestion point — either redact on the client side or configure server-side redaction rules. We have a per-route config to disable recording of full prompts for sensitive routes.
[05:12] Maya: On the network side: firewall rules. We need a minimal set of ports and FQDNs to allow. Can you give a short list?
[05:22] Alexei: Sure. For an in-VPC runtime: outbound to the control plane endpoint on 443 (TLS), intra-VPC RPC on high ports for model shards (configurable), and internal health/metrics endpoints if you want Prometheus scraping. If using our egress-proxy: allow proxy FQDN and proxy port, block others. We'll share a hardened ruleset doc.
[05:44] Priya: What about mTLS between runtime and control plane? Does Redwood support client cert rotate?
[05:52] Samira: Yes. We support mTLS with short-lived certs and automated rotation; certs can be issued by your internal CA, and we can integrate with EKS/Istio cert management.
[06:08] Maya: We need to explain to auditors how control plane telemetry can't access customer prompt text. Is there a separation between telemetry and payloads?
[06:18] Samira: Absolutely. Telemetry contains metrics, latencies, model version ids but not user PII. Payloads can remain in the runtime VPC and only metadata is sent to the control plane, unless you explicitly enable payload collection for debugging.
[06:34] Devon: About network egress logs — we want a single pane of truth for all egress flows with timestamped session records. Can Redwood forward flow logs?
[06:44] Alexei: We'll forward VPC flow logs and application-level logs to your SIEM; we can normalize them. Our recommended pattern is to enable VPC flow logs, RouteTable flow capture, and then have the egress-proxy produce more granular session records.
[06:58] Maya: In terms of proof, auditors will ask for SOC 2, penetration test reports, and ISO 27001 scope. Do you have those artifacts?
[07:08] Alexei: Yes — we provide SOC 2 Type II report for our control plane (and we can provide an attestation matrix for private deployments). We also maintain a public penetration testing summary and can deliver the full report under NDA. We'll attach links in the follow-up.
[07:24] Priya: About data residency — some customers require that keys and logs never leave EU. If we use cloud KMS in eu-west-1 and S3 buckets in the same region, is that sufficient?
[07:36] Samira: That covers most requirements. For extra assurance you can request our Private deployment to run entirely in your VPC and configure log endpoints in-region. Our telemetry collectors can be pointed to an in-region endpoint so no cross-region replication occurs.
[07:52] Devon: How about network segmentation inside the VPC — do you recommend separate subnets per model class or per sensitivity tier?
[08:00] Samira: Yes — separate subnets and security groups per sensitivity tier is best practice. Put PII-sensitive workloads in isolated subnets with stricter ACLs, and use the egress-proxy for all outbound. Also consider using host isolation via separate node pools if you're running on GKE/EKS.
[08:18] Maya: Can we do an air-gapped deployment where updates are applied via signed artifacts only, and no outbound control plane?
[08:26] Alexei: We have an air-gap option: you can host the control plane on-premise, and updates are delivered as signed tarballs via an approved channel. It requires additional ops work — not our default, but supported for high-regulated customers.
[08:40] Priya: For the PoC we want to measure latency and throughput with our average payloads. We also will need to exercise failover — for example, what happens if control plane is unreachable?
[08:50] Samira: If the control plane is unreachable, the runtime continues serving using cached model configuration and KV cache. We have configurable TTLs for config cache and automatic fallback policies to a local safety model. We'll include the failover behavior matrix in the follow-up doc.
[09:08] Devon: Also curious about telemetry sampling — we don't want to retain full prompts long-term. How do you recommend sampling?
[09:16] Samira: You can choose percentage sampling or route-based sampling. For audits we recommend route-based logging for a small set of demo prompts and sampling for high-volume endpoints.
[09:28] Maya: One more compliance question — can we get immutable logs (WORM) for audit windows?
[09:34] Alexei: Yes, using S3 object-lock in compliance mode or equivalent storage (GCS retention). We'll provide a recommended bucket policy for immutability.
[09:44] Priya: Are there any known limitations with Bring Your Own HSM?
[09:50] Samira: The main constraints are throughput and client drivers — PKCS#11 latencies can surface at high QPS. For high-throughput workloads we recommend a hybrid approach: customer-managed keys for long-term storage and a short-lived wrapping key for per-request speed. We'll include a performance note.
[10:10] [00:10:10] Speaker 2: (background) is there an expected cost delta for private with customer KMS?
[10:18] Alexei: There will be additional network egress and dedicated capacity charges; we'll include a cost comparison table in the follow up. Dedicated GPU pools also affect pricing.
[10:28] Maya: Ok great. On the evidence front, we need a mapping doc that ties each control to evidence artifacts that we can point to in an audit.
[10:36] Alexei: We'll supply a control-evidence mapping template — shows where the artifact lives (S3 link), retention policy, and owner.
[10:44] Devon: For the PoC, network wise we want a minimal setup: restricted VPC with a single NAT/egress-proxy, control plane in same VPC, and KMS in the same region. That will let us validate no-cross-region egress.
[10:58] Samira: Sounds good. We'll prepare a PoC runbook — steps to deploy the runtime, how to wire KMS, test payloads, and failover scenarios.
[11:08] Maya: Can you also include steps for SSO integration and a sample SAML metadata snippet?
[11:14] Alexei: Yes, Samira will include a SAML example and role mapping table.
[11:20] Priya: Thanks everyone. That covers our main concerns.
[11:24] Alexei: Quick recap of next steps — I'll send the security whitepaper + SOC2 and Samira will add network diagrams and a PoC runbook. Maya/Priya will share VectorHealth's compliance checklist and we'll schedule the PoC.
[11:40] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks.
[11:44] Alexei: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.

References/Links (mentioned during call):
